protections: On a redirect that leaves the original origin (scheme, host or port change), do not forward credential request headers sent to the original origin; Authorization is the reported value and Cookie is the same class of credential in the later incomplete-fix advisory, while same-origin redirects must still carry them.

The removal set must be carried as Retry policy (default plus per-request configuration) so it applies to the default retries object and survives Retry.new()/increment() on multi-hop redirects, and the same rule must hold in each redirect-following implementation in the package (PoolManager, HTTPConnectionPool, AppEngineManager).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The advisory and the report name only the Authorization header; Cookie is a separate header carrying a separate credential and nothing in the report puts cookies in scope.

One hardcoded Authorization strip satisfies the demonstrated case; the retry object's defaults and per-hop rebuild are internal details, and the report never asks for a configurable removal set or for settings to survive a multi-hop chain.

HTTPConnectionPool is a single-host pool: assert_same_host defaults to True and raises HostChangedError, so a cross-host redirect is reachable only when a caller explicitly passes assert_same_host=False, which the docs reserve for proxy use.

The Location is joined to an absolute URL before a guard would run and most redirects keep the scheme; comparing the parsed host (or the raw URL string) is assumed to be enough, so default-port, mixed-case host, IPv6 and same-host scheme/port-change shapes look like edge cases.

Every hop of a proxied request goes to the same proxy, so the connection pool is a stable reference and stripping whenever the redirect target differs from the pool looks conservative: it over-strips but does not under-strip.
App Engine's urlfetch follows redirects inside the platform, this manager is legacy platform-specific contrib code, and the library cannot see intermediate hops without disabling follow_redirects.

conflicts.what: The crude fix for T1 - delete the header on every redirect - satisfies the cross-origin check but breaks the same-origin half of T5: relative Location values and default-port or mixed-case same-origin redirects must keep Authorization/Cookie, and the recursion at poolmanager.py:349 re-sends whatever survives unless the origin test is shape-correct.

Broadening removal to Cookie and keying the origin test on the connection pool (the predicate the code offers at connectionpool.py:428) over-strips: for plain-HTTP ProxyManager requests the pool is the proxy (poolmanager.py:402-408), so a same-origin target redirect looks cross-origin and must-keep credentials are removed.

Hardcoding Cookie into the strip is the natural fix for T2 but contradicts T3's configurable removal set: a caller who passes an empty or custom set must be able to keep Cookie/Authorization or remove a different credential header, which a hardcoded list cannot express.

fairness_risks: Same-origin redirects (relative Location such as '/next', default-port forms, same host different case) must still carry Authorization and Cookie; a rule that strips on every redirect breaks authenticated redirect chains. The pinned recursion at poolmanager.py:315-316 and 349 is what preserves them today, and connectionpool.py:441-447 exists precisely to normalise those shapes.

PoolManager(headers=...) and ProxyManager(headers=..., proxy_headers=...) are shared configuration. kw['headers'] aliases self.headers at poolmanager.py:315-316, so deleting from it in place silently removes the header from every later request made by that manager; the fix must copy before removing.

Users must be able to opt out or customise: keep a header cross-origin with an empty removal set, or add a non-standard credential header (for example X-Api-Key) to the removal set. A hardcoded Authorization-only (or Authorization+Cookie-only) rule contradicts both legitimate uses.

ProxyManager deliberately reuses the proxy's pool for every plain-HTTP target (poolmanager.py:402-408), so a security rule that treats the pool as the origin will refuse to keep credentials on same-origin redirects that must keep working.

Some applications rely on the Cookie header surviving a redirect to a sibling host or subdomain; the origin rule will stop that, so a documented opt-out (the custom removal set) is needed rather than silently widening or narrowing the default.

design.why: The reported surface T1 is the easy anchor: the PoolManager redirect recursion re-sends kw['headers'] at poolmanager.py:349 with no origin comparison, so any solver finds it. The stack adds four independent judgements with different reasons to dismiss. T2: the same guard must remove Cookie, not only the header the report names; this is the later published incomplete-fix bug, and a solver reading the advisory literally leaves it open (deepseek-type: protection absent plus a report-scope reason to dismiss). T3: the removal set must live on Retry defaults and be copied by new()/increment() so it applies to the default retries object and survives multi-hop chains; it is a different file, and a hardcoded one-hop strip passes a naive test (deepseek-type). T4: HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen is a second redirect implementation that never receives the manager's guard, reachable through documented assert_same_host=False use, with a strong single-host reason to dismiss (deepseek-type). T6: ProxyManager substitutes the proxy pool for the target origin at poolmanager.py:402-408, so an origin check keyed on the connection pool over-strips same-origin proxied redirects - the coupled must-keep value sitting next to the hidden cross-origin one (mimo-type over-hardening). The design spans poolmanager.py, util/retry.py and connectionpool.py, covers both the deepseek and mimo failure modes, and stays inside one advisory concept; T5 is a shape refinement of the T1/T2 guard (same group) and T7 is a third implementation that is hard to grade because google.appengine.api is unavailable outside App Engine.

unverified: The pinned commit c4f123dc predates both published fixes; a_fix 560bd227 and b_fix adb358f8e068 are not present in the tree (no header-removal name exists under urllib3/), so the A/B split and the claim that A's guard covered only Authorization are taken from the advisory pair and fix ids, not read from code.

Mapping GHSA-gwvm-45gx-3cf8 to the 2023 Cookie-header-leak advisory (the incomplete fix of CVE-2018-20060) is inferred from the 2023-10-15 publication date, the 'incomplete fix' link and the paired fix commit; no advisory text is present in the checkout.

The exact API shape of the reference fix (a Retry-level default removal set such as DEFAULT_REMOVE_HEADERS_ON_REDIRECT and a per-request option) is inferred from the pinned Retry design; the pinned tree contains no such field, so whether hidden tests exercise custom removal sets or multi-hop propagation was not verifiable.
Upstream coverage of the connectionpool and appengine redirect paths (marked uncovered_upstream) was not checked against a newer urllib3 checkout.
The same-origin behaviour of the reference fixes (strip only cross-origin versus strip on every redirect) could not be read here; the conflicts describe the risk under either implementation.
AppEngineManager cannot be exercised without google.appengine.api (the import is guarded at urllib3/contrib/appengine.py:62-65), so a trap there may not be gradeable even though it is real.
That both fixes are in-repo rather than dependency bumps is inferred from the candidate metadata naming commits of this repository; those commits are not readable from the pinned worktree.
